passage:
Thursday night
Told Gurleen about the promotion today. I almost didn't. At my last job, when I got a raise, two people stopped eating lunch with me, so I've learned to keep good news small.
But Gurleen just lit up. She actually hugged me in the corridor, then made the whole team sing a terrible congratulations song in the pantry. No 'lucky you' face, no jokes about who I must have impressed. Just glad.
Walking home, I felt lighter than I have in months. I even told her about the bigger thing I want: to run the Pune office one day. Out loud. First time.
Note to self: Gurleen's exam results are out in March. Be as loud as she was.
— Kishore

passage: At the zilla parishad school in Wai, the staffroom was a single table under a fan that clicked. When the circular came, Anjali, twenty-four and in her second year, read it twice before saying anything. She had been chosen as block resource teacher for reading. Her old school had taught her to keep news like that quiet; there, a colleague had once said, "Some people know how to please the right officers." So she only said, softly, "They picked me for the block training." Joseph Sir, who had taught there for twenty years, put down his tea. "Anjali! That's wonderful. You earned it with those reading circles." He called the peon to bring pedhas. Anjali felt her shoulders loosen. Before she knew it, she was telling him her whole plan for a village library. Months later, when Joseph Sir's own science project was chosen, she was the first to clap.

qa.q: What was Anjali chosen as?
qa.a: Block resource teacher for reading.

qa.q: How did Anjali feel when Joseph Sir called for pedhas?
qa.a: She felt safe and relaxed, her shoulders loosening, enough to share her whole plan openly.

qa.q: What turning point made Anjali open up, and what did it lead to later?
qa.a: Joseph Sir's sincere gladness; it led her to share her library plan and later be the first to celebrate his project.

qa.q: How might Joseph Sir see his reaction to Anjali's news?
qa.a: He probably saw it as simply fair and natural to be happy for a young teacher who earned it, not as anything special.

passage: Abebe almost didn't mention it. At the small engineering firm in Toronto, he'd learned to keep wins quiet; at his last job, good news had brought jokes about luck and who he knew. But on Monday, at the coffee machine, Yara asked how his weekend was, and it slipped out: his first design had been accepted for a city bridge repair. Yara put down her mug. "Abebe, that's huge. Your first real public project!" She meant it; he could see it. She made him show her the drawings on his phone, and asked so many questions that he forgot to be nervous. By lunch he was sketching out his bigger idea for the next tender, the one he'd never told anyone. In March, when Yara's research grant came through, Abebe bought the whole office cake.

qa.a: Abebe's first design.
